snapshot.title: TNPSC Unit 8: Sangam Age — Literature & Society
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC Unit 8 Hook: Silappathikaram: Ilango. Kurinji: Murugan. Keezhadi: Vaigai. 3rd Sangam: Madurai. Pathupattu: 10 songs.

quick_notes.title: Sangam Assemblies
quick_notes.detail: 1. First (Thenmadurai), 2. Second (Kapatapuram), 3. Third (Madurai - most surviving works from here).
quick_notes.explanation: Sangam Assemblies were three ancient Tamil literary gatherings held in South India over many centuries. The First Sangam was held at Thenmadurai, a city now lost, but no books from it survive today. The Second Sangam took place at Kapatapuram, which was also destroyed by the sea, and only a few poems remain from this meeting. The Third and most famous Sangam was held at Madurai, a city that still exists, and almost all of the Tamil poems and stories we have today, like the Ettuthokai and the Pathupattu, come from this final assembly.

quick_notes.title: Five Thinai (Landscapes)
quick_notes.detail: Kurinji (Mountains - Murugan), Mullai (Forest - Thirumal), Marutham (Agricultural - Indiran), Neithal (Coastal - Varunan), Palai (Desert - Korravai).
quick_notes.explanation: The Five Thinai is a system from ancient Tamil Sangam literature that divides the land into five distinct landscapes, each with its own god, people, and way of life. Kurinji is the mountain region, and its chief god is Murugan, also known as the god of war and youth. Mullai is the forest region, and its chief god is Thirumal, who is the same as Vishnu, the preserver god. Marutham is the agricultural plain, and its chief god is Indiran, the god of rain and king of the gods. Neithal is the coastal region, and its chief god is Varunan, the god of the sea and water. Palai is the desert or wasteland, and its chief god is Korravai, the goddess of victory and war.

quick_notes.title: Pathupattu & Ettuthogai
quick_notes.detail: The core 18 works. Famous : Maduraikanchi, Nedunalvaadai, Purananuru (Heroism), Agananuru (Love).
quick_notes.explanation: Pathupattu and Ettuthogai are two collections that together make up the core eighteen works of ancient Tamil Sangam literature. Pathupattu, meaning "Ten Idylls," is a set of ten long poems that describe landscapes, seasons, and emotions. Ettuthogai, meaning "Eight Anthologies," is a set of eight shorter poem collections. Famous works include Maduraikanchi and Nedunalvaadai from the Pathupattu, and Purananuru, which focuses on heroism and war, and Agananuru, which focuses on love and relationships, from the Ettuthogai.

quick_notes.title: Twin Epics
quick_notes.detail: Silappathikaram (Ilango Adigal - Kovalan/Kannagi) and Manimegalai (Sathanar - daughter of Kovalan).
quick_notes.explanation: The Twin Epics are two famous ancient Tamil poems. The first is Silappathikaram, written by the poet Ilango Adigal. It tells the story of a merchant named Kovalan and his faithful wife Kannagi. After Kovalan is wrongly executed for stealing a queen's anklet, Kannagi proves his innocence by breaking her other anklet, which contains a ruby, and then curses the city of Madurai, causing it to burn. The second epic is Manimegalai, written by the poet Sathanar. It continues the story by focusing on Manimegalai, who is the daughter of Kovalan and a dancer named Madhavi. Manimegalai becomes a Buddhist nun and performs miracles, such as using a magical bowl to feed the hungry.

quick_notes.title: Archaeological Sites
quick_notes.detail: Keezhadi (Sivagangai - Urban life), Adichanallur (Thoothukudi - Urns), Arikamedu (Puducherry - Roman trade).
quick_notes.explanation: Here is your lesson on Archaeological Sites. An archaeological site is a place where old things from the past, like tools or buildings, are found buried in the ground. Keezhadi, located in the Sivagangai district, is a site that shows us evidence of a very old urban life, meaning people lived there in a city-like settlement with streets and houses. Adichanallur, located in the Thoothukudi district, is a site famous for its large burial urns, which are big clay pots used by ancient people to store the bones of their dead. Arikamedu, located in the Puducherry region, is a site that provides clear proof of trade between ancient India and the Roman Empire, as many Roman-made pots and beads have been found there.
